steps.label: KP04 One Perceptron cannot solve XOR
The four XOR points · 1/8
steps.speakerNotes: The four XOR points: 0 0 and 1 1 are class 0; 0 1 and 1 0 are class 1.

steps.label: The four XOR points · 1/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The two points of a class sit exactly on a diagonal of the square.

steps.label: The four XOR points · 1/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Chapter 1 already proved no weights make XOR. For the learning rule, KP02's conclusion reverses: not separable means it never stops.

steps.label: The four XOR points · 1/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: KP02's conclusion, reversed separable → guaranteed to stop not separable → never stops Chapter 1 proved it: no w_1,w_2,w_0 makes XOR

steps.label: Running XOR · 2/8
steps.speakerNotes: Start from zeros and learn XOR in order with learning rate 1. The first two passes make 3 updates each.

steps.label: Running XOR · 2/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: From the third pass every pass makes 4 updates, through pass ten.

steps.label: Running XOR · 2/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: From pass four on every pass ends at the same weights minus 1, 0, 0: four updates inside a pass loop back to the start, so there is never a pass without an update.

steps.label: Running XOR · 2/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: from pass 4 on, every pass ends at the same (w_1,w_2,w_0)=(-1,0,0) a pass with no update never happens

steps.label: Grid search · 3/8
steps.speakerNotes: One neuron's boundary is a straight line; however you draw it, some point is wrong.

steps.label: Grid search · 3/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: A program evaluates all 343 weight triples on the integer grid from minus 3 to plus 3.

steps.label: Grid search · 3/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: At most 3 of 4 are right. This is not too little data or a bad learning rate; it is a limit of expressiveness.

steps.label: Grid search · 3/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: at most only 3 / 4 not too little data or a bad learning rate: a limit of expressiveness

steps.label: The start decides · 4/8
steps.speakerNotes: Two classes, linearly separable; same data, same rule.

steps.label: The start decides · 4/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Changing only the start and the data order gives boundary A and boundary B. Both have training error 0. The blobs here are schematic.

steps.label: The start decides · 4/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: But for the new point 2.5, 2.4 the two lines disagree. The Perceptron stops at all-right and never picks the best one.

steps.label: The start decides · 4/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: new point (2.5,2.4) both lines have training error 0 they differ only in start and data order: the Perceptron stops at all-right and does not pick the best line all-right only means it stopped, not that it stopped well

steps.label: Opposite answers · 5/8
steps.speakerNotes: Boundary A has weights 4.03, 3.17 and bias minus 15.22. At the new point s is 2.46, so class 1.

steps.label: Opposite answers · 5/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Boundary B has weights 0.94, 0.95 and bias minus 5.04. At the new point s is minus 0.41, so class 0.

steps.label: Opposite answers · 5/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Both are perfect on the training data yet give opposite answers on the new point. Zero training error does not imply generalization.

steps.label: Opposite answers · 5/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: both are 100% right on training data: which do you trust? unseen data must decide (validation, later) zero training error does not imply generalization

steps.label: History · 6/8
steps.speakerNotes: In 1958 Rosenblatt proposed the Perceptron, the first neuron that learns.

steps.label: History · 6/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: In 1960 Widrow and Hoff proposed ADALINE, using a continuous LMS loss.

steps.label: History · 6/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: In 1969 Minsky and Papert analyzed the single-layer limit, and XOR became the best-known counterexample. The way out afterwards was multiple layers with nonlinear activation.

steps.label: History · 6/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Chapter 1 reminded us: the XOR limit is a checkable mathematical fact, but a single book causing a whole research winter is an oversimplification.

steps.label: History · 6/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: “one book caused a whole winter” oversimplifies; the XOR limit itself is a checkable fact

steps.label: Two ways out · 7/8
steps.speakerNotes: The first limit: the boundary is only a straight line.

steps.label: Two ways out · 7/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The way out is layers with nonlinear activation, the next unit KP05.

steps.label: Two ways out · 7/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The second limit: the Perceptron wants all-right and does not pick the best line.

steps.label: Two ways out · 7/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The way out is a method that picks a good line, such as ADALINE with a continuous loss, in KP08.

steps.label: Two ways out · 7/8 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: way out ADALINE with a continuous loss (KP08) structure fixes the line limit; a different loss fixes the generalization limit

steps.label: Summary and question · 8/8
steps.speakerNotes: First myth: separable data means the Perceptron learns well. Separable only guarantees it stops, not where.

steps.label: Summary and question · 8/8 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second myth: XOR fails because of too little data or a bad rate. No, it is a limit of expressiveness.

steps.label: Summary and question · 8/8 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: For the next unit: XOR is at least one is 1 and not both are 1. Can we connect several neurons?

steps.label: Summary and question · 8/8 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: XOR can be written “at least one is 1, and not both are 1”. Can we connect several neurons so that one's output is the next one's input? next unit: stack neurons into layers
